Whenever Orion commits a change to a cacheable record, the database publishes an invalidation event to Aurora.
Helios consumes invalidation events from Aurora and removes the corresponding cached records.
Orion first commits the database transaction and then writes an outbox record in the same transaction.
The Relay Service reads the outbox, publishes the invalidation event to Aurora, and marks the outbox record as delivered.
The Relay Service reads the outbox record and uses it to publish pending invalidation events.
Helios removes the affected key from the primary partition and its replicas after receiving the invalidation event.
If the Relay Service temporarily stops, the outbox retains undelivered events until it restarts.
When the Relay Service is down, delayed invalidations may extend the lifetime of stale cache entries, but the request is not permanently lost.

During early load tests, the team observed a cache stampede, motivating cache stampede protection.
When a popular record expired, hundreds of Meridian workers missed the same key at nearly the same time.
Each miss triggered a separate Orion query, temporarily recreating the original database load problem.
Maya introduced request coalescing to prevent the cache stampede behavior.
The first miss for a key creates an in-flight fetch.
Later requests for the same key wait for the existing fetch instead of starting additional database queries.
When Orion returns the record, Helios completes the cache fill and releases all waiting requests with the same value.

To limit stalled requests, Helios applies a fetch timeout of eight hundred milliseconds.

On March 18, the team conducted a production-scale load test that increased Atlas traffic to fifteen million events per hour.
The load test intentionally terminated one Helios primary node.
The replica promotion completed successfully, but Meridian latency rose sharply several minutes later.
Owen opened an incident channel after Meridian latency rose sharply.
Owen asked each service owner to report current metrics in the incident channel, and Sentinel reported a drop in Helios hit rate.
Sentinel showed that Orion query volume had tripled.
The Relay Service appeared healthy when service owners reported current metrics in the incident channel.
Luis discovered that most of the additional Orion queries involved permission records.
Priya reviewed the deployment configuration for the replacement nodes.
A malformed environment variable was interpreted as milliseconds by one component and seconds by another, creating the bad expiration setting in the deployment configuration.
The short expiration caused frequent misses for permission records.
Request coalescing could not fully protect Orion because permission requests were distributed across many different keys.
The team corrected the configuration and restarted the affected replacement nodes.

Because Helios serves many customer accounts, the security team performed dedicated tenant-isolation tests.
The tenant-isolation tests generated identical equipment identifiers under different accounts and verified that cache lookups returned the correct account-specific records.
One test revealed that a debugging endpoint accepted a cache key without independently verifying the authenticated account.
The debugging endpoint was available only inside the engineering network, but it could still expose metadata if an internal credential were misused.
Priya disabled the debugging endpoint immediately after the test revealed the authentication gap.
Maya replaced the debugging endpoint with a diagnostic operation that derives the account identifier from the authenticated request rather than accepting it from user input.
